text: I now give the floor to her excellency
Maria Teresa Lazaro, Secretary of
Foreign Affairs of the Philippines,
>> Mr. President, excellencies, we meet at
a perilous precipice, a tumultuous time
marked by profound upheaval, relentless
uncertainty, and deep unpredictability.
More than 50 active conflicts tear
tear of the fabric of nations.
Geopolitical competition strains our
multilateral institutions and global
trust is fading precisely when we need
it most. 81 years ago, our forebears
forged this organization to save
humanity from the scourge of war and
reaffirm our shared dignity. Today, we
must ask, have we honored that sacred
compact? When more than 645 million
people face hunger, when our climate
remains in a state of calamity, and when
our collective conscience is stained by
humanitarian catastrophes,
reflection must give way to urgent
united resolve. We cannot continue down
fragmented paths. In an interconnected
world, the disruption of maritime
traffic in the Middle East can trigger
an energy emergency in the Philippines.
More than 3,600 nautical miles away, the
war in Ukraine compounds a global food
crisis and economic shocks unseen since
the Second World War. Peace, therefore,
is not merely the absence of war. It is
our shared and individual indivisible
responsibility.
reiterate our call for an immediate and
sustained ceasefire in Gaza, the
protection of civilians, the release of
all hostages, and full compliance by all
parties with international law,
including international humanitarian
law. We urge all relevant parties to
deescalate, exercise restraint, and
return to the path of dialogue.
The Philippines reaffirms its consistent
and principled support for the
inalienable right of the Palestinian
people to self-determination.
We firmly believe that the two-state
solution remains the only viable path to
lasting and durable peace with Israel
and Palestine living side by side in
peace and security and all others
respecting their peaceful coexistence.
Peace is a daily choice. It requires
diplomacy, justice, respect for
international law, confidence building,
and sustained investment in conflict
prevention and peace building with the
United Nations at the heart of this
effort. Mr. President, excellencies,
numbers and statistics can obscure the
true magnitude of our trials. Behind
every metric is a human story. Put a
face to the climate emergency. A single
disaster can erase decades of hardwarned
progress. Look at Nepal bearing the
heavy cost of rising temperatures
despite contributing less than 0.1%
of global emissions. Look to the
Philippines, one of the world's most
climate vulnerable nations. Since August
alone,
ferocious monsoons and storms have
battered our islands, affecting more
than 2.7 million families, destroying
homes and shattering livelihoods.
We share this vulnerabilities with many
developing countries, particularly small
islands and coastal states. Those who
have contributed less to the climate
crisis must now bear its heaviest cost.
We call for the effective implementation
of the Paris agreement, the full
operationalization of the fund for
responding to loss and damage and
strengthened implementation of the SAI
framework. Put the face to the pursuit
of sustainable development. With the
2030 agenda less than four years away,
only 36% of accessible SDG targets are
on track. Achieving these goals requires
renewed political will, stronger
partnerships with the private sector,
reform of the international financial
architecture, and a United Nations
development system responsive to the
evolving needs and priorities of
developing countries. Consistent with
the compromiso de civilia, we call for
stronger international cooperation to
mobilize development financing,
facilitate technology transfer, and
strengthen capacity building.
As a country that has newly attained
upper middle income status, the
Philippines knows that income
classification is not the end of the
journey. Our metrics must evolve to
capture the structural vulnerabilities,
debt burdens, and inequalities that
continue to affect middle inome
countries. Put a face to the digital
revolution and to the rise of artificial
intelligence. We stand at the dawn of an
unprecedented technological era.
harnessed responsibly frontier
technologies and AI can accelerate
sustainable development, optimize
resources and bridge deep global
divides. But AI also presents profound
and systemic risks. Without robust
governance and forcible ethical
standards and strong legal guard rails,
it could deepen inequalities and become
an existential challenge. We echo the
growing call across industries that we
need robust AI governance with
enforcable standards. And we need it
now.
Advanced capabilities must never be
allowed to pose unacceptable risks to
human lives, human rights or democratic
integrity.
Effective governance must also address
deep developmental asymmetries. We are
not entering the AI era from the same
starting point. Managing this revolution
requires closing critical gaps in
digital infrastructure, computing
resources, and technical expertise so
that developing countries are not left
behind. We need AI systems that uplift
the vulnerable, strengthen national
resilience, promote gender equality, and
foster human- centered partnerships, not
exclusion and fragmentation. Put a face
to the tireless migrant workers and
seafarers who keep the global community
afloat.
Millions of migrant workers leave their
homes to search for a better life,
contributing immeasurably to the
sustainable development of countries of
origin, transit, and destination.
They are committed to full human rights
and fundamental freedoms regardless of
status and deserve steadfast protection
from trafficking and exploitation along
perilous migration routes. Among them,
our seafarers form an indispensable
lifeline of global commerce. Nearly 90%
of world trade moves by sea, supported
by close to 2 million seafarers, more
than 25% of whom are Filipinos. They are
essential workers yet increasingly
vulnerable to conflict and attacks at
sea. Just recently, an incident in the
street of Haruz claimed the lives of
Filipino seafares and endured many
others.
Their tragedy reminds us that maritime
security is human security. Put a face
to our identities and archipelagic and
maritime nation where open and secure
seas are our lifeblood. For the
Philippines, the safety of ships and
seafares cannot be separated from supply
chains and global commerce.
Open and secure seas free from
interference and coercion are vital to
our security, our economy and our
people. International law must remain
our guiding lighthouse with UNLOS the UN
universal um declaration the common on
the law of the sea convention on the law
of the sea standing firmly as the
constitution of the oceans. Next year
marks the 45th anniversary of UNLOS and
the Manila declaration on the peaceful
settlement of international disputes.
This year also marks a decade since the
2016 South China Sea Arbitial Award, an
award that is final and legally binding
and that demonstrates how international
law provides states with peaceful means
to clarify rights and resolve
differences. The Philippines stands firm
in its conviction that disputes must be
resolved through diplomacy and law, not
violence and might.
International cooperation to protect
maritime security must also extend to
critical maritime infrastructure, the
physical and digital nervous system of
our shared prosperity. From undersea
cables carrying 90% of global data to
strategic sea lanes and ports sustaining
trade to offshore facilities fueling
economies, disruption of critical
maritime infrastructure can send shock
waves across borders. Rather than
waiting for threats and asking who
should respond, states must explore a
framework anchored on UNC law clause
that sets out clear rules, rights, and
obligations governing critical maritime
infrastructure.
Mr. President, excellencies, all our
advancements will falter if they are not
they are not anchored in universal human
rights and safeguarded from the shadow
of modern threats. Since joining the
United Nations as a founding member, the
Philippines has proudly stood with the
vanguards of human rights. We advocated
decolonization and the elimination of
discrimination against women. We
advanced the rights of children, persons
with disabilities, older persons,
indigenous peoples, and migrants. And we
called firmly for an end to upper tide
and all forms of racial discrimination.
We will continue to champion these
timeless principles. At the same time,
we must secure our future by ensuring
responsible behavior in outer space,
reducing space threats, and preventing
an arms race in outer space. We also
urge a renewed and rigorous commitment
to nonprololiferation treaty, the
cornerstone of the global nuclear
disarmament and non-prololiferation
architecture. Restoring trust in the NPT
is imperative if we are to achieve our
shared vision of a world free from
existential threat of nuclear weapons.
Closer to home, the Philippines own
journey toward lasting peace,
exemplified by the Banksamoro Autonomous
Region in Muslim Mindanao has taught us
an invaluable lesson. Lasting peace
requires addressing the root causes of
conflict, empowering local communities,
and ensuring that women are at the
center of peace building. Mr. President,
excellencies, our world is evolving. So
must the United Nations. To remain
effective, we must reform the Security
Council to make it more representative,
transparent, and accountable. expanding
the voices of developing regions across
Asia, Africa, Latin America, and the
Caribbean. As we look to the future, we
are reminded that everything we strive
for ultimately depends on how we choose
to navigate these trials together. We we
need to reflect deeply on the promises
of our charter and on the state of our
fractured world. We must actively seek
collective pathways that transcend
borders and bridge divides. And above
all, we must always put a face to what
we do, remembering that every policy,
every treaty, and every institutional
reform is ultimately about real human
lives. It is in this spirit that we
voice a historic aspiration, the hope
for a woman secretary general, a leader
who can rally nations back to true
multilateralism and deliver for all.
Thank you very much.
I thank the Secretary of Foreign Affairs
of the Philippines.
